analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the 20% tax deduction for pass-through business owners' income.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote, despite sponsorship from 34 of 49 Senate Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law created a deduction worth 20% of income from businesses that are not corporations — partnerships, S-corporations, and sole proprietorships. That deduction is set to expire after 2025. This bill would remove the expiration date, making the deduction permanent. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of pass-through businesses — including law firms, real estate partnerships, hedge funds, and other professional practices — keep a deduction worth 20% of their business income indefinitely. Independent analyses of the deduction have found its benefits flow disproportionately to high-earning business owners, since the deduction scales with income and most workers' wages do not qualify.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the December 31, 2025 expiration date on the qualified business income deduction, so owners of non-corporate businesses keep a 20% deduction on that income permanently rather than seeing it lapse.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dollar claimed as a deduction is revenue the government does not collect, which must be made up through borrowing, other taxes, or reduced spending. Because the deduction's benefits concentrate among high-income business owners, the general body of taxpayers effectively backstops a tax break that mostly reaches the top.

drawbacks.text: Making the deduction permanent reduces federal revenue indefinitely, increasing deficits or forcing offsetting cuts and tax increases elsewhere — a cost borne by taxpayers at large.

The deduction only applies to business income, not wages, so salaried workers get nothing from it while high-earning owners of law firms, hedge funds, and real estate partnerships benefit in proportion to their income. Critics have long noted this favors business income over work income, and can even create incentives to restructure salaries as business distributions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives certainty to pass-through business owners planning around the 2025 sunset, which has real value for a small-business owner's planning. But the permanent cost falls on the Treasury, and the benefit is heavily tilted toward the highest-earning business owners rather than typical small operators, who often have too little income to owe much tax anyway. It is a large, permanent tax preference for one category of high income.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Daines introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, with 14 original Republican cosponsors, to make the qualified business income deduction permanent by striking its expiration clause.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind on the bill.
The bill's deduction was set to lapse after December 31, 2025 under current law, and the bill would have removed that sunset.
The bill ended the 118th Congress with 34 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one acted on the bill, so the scheduled 2025 expiration of the deduction remained in place and the Treasury retained the revenue the permanence would have surrendered; high-earning pass-through owners did not get the certainty they sought. (The question was later revisited in the next Congress.)

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the qualified business income deduction permanent.

for.name: 34 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or independent did.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action, it had no path forward.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Republicans out of 49 Senate Republicans; no Democrat or independent signed on, and the Democratic-controlled chamber never acted on it.

industries.industry: Pass-through businesses (law firms, hedge funds, real estate and private equity partnerships, S-corporations)
industries.note: The bill would permanently preserve a 20% deduction on their business income, a benefit scaled to income and concentrated among the highest-earning owners. The cost is federal revenue that other taxpayers ultimately backstop.
